title: Structural Traps — Resource Deadlock
metadata_mapping: Existing concept and responsive asset conventions; no new schema, navigation, or publication action.

patterns.title: Resource Deadlock
patterns.domain: Dependency and feasibility traps: reusable-resource allocation and circular waiting

sources.title: E. G. Coffman Jr., M. J. Elphick, A. Shoshani (1971), System Deadlocks
sources.supports: Original twelve-page survey read in a university teaching mirror: introduction and pp. 70–74 on necessary conditions, resource multiplicity, prevention, detection, and recovery. Original venue Computing Surveys 3(2):67–78.
sources.boundary: Foundational synthesis of earlier work, not sole origin and not a trial of organizational interventions. The controlled traffic scenario is original and hypothetical.

current_example_check.read: Figure 1 and surrounding discussion, printed p. 69, explicitly map traffic around a square to held-space and next-space requests.
current_example_check.boundary: The safe-bay recovery and entry control are this article’s hypothetical additions.

sources.title: University of Illinois CS 341 coursebook, Deadlock
sources.supports: Coffman conditions, single-instance allocation cycles, common ordering, and opposite-order release/retry livelock.
sources.boundary: Only those standard model claims are used. No assertion is taken from the page’s broader operating-system or undecidability discussion.

sources.title: John Bell, Operating Systems: Deadlocks, University of Illinois Chicago
sources.supports: Multiple-instance counterexample, prevention costs, bundle allocation, declared maximum demands, safe sequences, and unsafe versus already deadlocked states.
sources.boundary: Identifiable teaching notes based on Operating System Concepts, ninth edition; no empirical effect sizes or current operating-system behavior are inferred.

sources.title: PostgreSQL 18 documentation, 13.3.4 Deadlocks
sources.supports: Opposite-order account-row updates, automatic deadlock detection and victim abortion, unpredictable victim selection, consistent ordering, and retry of aborted transactions.
sources.boundary: Official product behavior and worked documentation example, not an observed intervention study or a guarantee about arbitrary lock types or external side effects.

patterns.short_description: Trace who holds each needed resource, break a closed chain of waiting safely, and change allocation rules to prevent the same deadlock from returning.
use_when: Which held space prevents each driver from moving?
goals: Recognize the concrete predicament before terminology.
Preserve defining assumptions and distinctions without calculations.
Evaluate intervention authority, costs, residual risks, and changed assumptions.
mechanisms: Create a safe release, then prevent new entry from closing the cycle again.
Safe geometry, authority, and compliance are assumed. No road-control specification is supplied.

example_structure.scenario: Four distinct cars hold four exclusive spaces and require the next held space before forward release. No ordinary gap or escape. Recovery explicitly adds an authorized safe bay movement and controls new entry; no road engineering prescription. Single-instance resource result kept separate from multi-instance systems.
example_structure.changed_relationship: Create a safe release, then prevent new entry from closing the cycle again.
example_structure.residual_constraints: Safe geometry, authority, and compliance are assumed. No road-control specification is supplied.
example_structure.evidence: Hypothetical scenario and stipulated continuation; no expected result presented as measured outcome. Qualitative ranking and ordering replace illustrative arithmetic.

visual.question: Which held space prevents each driver from moving?
visual.alternative_text: Hypothetical qualitative illustration. A holds A and requests B; B holds B and requests C; C holds C and requests D; D holds D and requests A. No ordinary forward move is available. Authorized removal of A to a safe bay frees A, allowing D, C, and B to move before A can re-enter. Change: Create a safe release, then prevent new entry from closing the cycle again. Limitation: Safe geometry, authority, and compliance are assumed. No road-control specification is supplied.
visual.caption: Hypothetical illustration. The upper arrows are requests for occupied spaces, not directions on a road map. The lower sequence creates a gap and keeps new entry from consuming it. A safe bay and controlled movement are additional capabilities, and A loses priority.
